title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi's farewell, Ganpati Bappa Morya. Welcome it, then let it go.

On the same autumn day, in three corners of India, three different things are happening. In a Delhi park, a crowd watches a giant paper-and-bamboo Ravana, taller than a house, as someone fires a flaming arrow into it. In Kolkata, married women smear red sindoor on each other's faces, laughing and crying, before an image of Durga about to leave for the river. In a Kerala home, a small child writes their first letters in a plate of rice. It's all one day: the tenth.
screen: `A BURNING RAVANA IN DELHI.` → `RED SINDOOR IN KOLKATA.` → `FIRST LETTERS IN KERALA.`

segments.voice: The tenth day after the nine nights is Vijayadashami, the victory tenth. In much of North India it's called Dussehra, and it belongs to Rama. For the nine nights before, many towns stage the Ramlila, the whole Ramayana acted over many evenings. On the tenth day, Rama defeats Ravana, and huge effigies of Ravana, often with his brothers Kumbhakarna and Meghanada, are burned. In Bengal, the same day is Bijoya Dashami, the end of Durga Puja. The Goddess, who people there say has been visiting her parents' home with her children, goes back to Shiva. Before her image is carried to the river, women offer her sweets and sindoor, then smear it on one another, a custom called sindoor khela. Afterward people embrace and visit, and the young touch the feet of the old. In much of the South, the ninth and tenth days honor tools and learning. On Ayudha Puja, people clean and decorate their tools, books, vehicles, even laptops, and set them before the Goddess. On Vijayadashami, especially in Kerala, many small children begin their education, writing their first letters in rice or sand with an elder guiding their finger. One day, three victories: the good over Ravana, the Goddess over Mahisha, the mind over not-knowing. And this week has been full of nights ending in dawn: Diwali before sunrise in the South, Holi's colors in Braj, the blue throat, Shachi's thread, a baby girl who couldn't be held, a farewell that means come back, and now the tenth day.
screen: `VIJAYADASHAMI: THE VICTORY TENTH.` · `DUSSEHRA: RAVANA BURNS.` · `BIJOYA: DURGA GOES HOME.` · `FIRST LETTERS WRITTEN IN RICE.` · then, large: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Place in front of you, or picture, one tool you use every day: a pen, a phone, your own hands. Look at it the way people on Ayudha Puja look at their tools, with thanks. Then name one small thing you won't let win tonight, and let the breath carry a quiet decision.
Navaratri. Nine nights that end on Vijayadashami: Ravana burned in the North, Durga's farewell in Bengal, tools and first letters honored in the South.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. A child's first letter counts as a victory too. Day six hundred eighty-six, done.
